definitions.definition: The specific moment when a system breaks into separate, opposing parts.
definitions.example: Like the exact second a glass window cracks from a rock hit.

definitions.definition: A measure of how different the words and phrases used by one political party are from the other party's.
definitions.example: If Democrats always say 'climate crisis' and Republicans always say 'energy freedom,' that's high distinctiveness.

definitions.definition: Separate worlds of meaning where the same words have different meanings for different groups.
definitions.example: Like how 'freedom' means 'no government rules' to one person and 'healthcare for all' to another.

definitions.definition: Coming after or as a result of something else, not the cause.
definitions.example: If you decide what to eat based on your mood, your food choice is downstream of your mood.

definitions.definition: Being the cause or source of something, not the result.
definitions.example: Your mood is upstream of your food choice if your mood decides what you eat.

definitions.definition: Ways of doing things that are chosen mainly because they signal which group you belong to, not because they are the best way.
definitions.example: Wearing a certain brand of sneakers not because they're comfortable but because your friends wear them.

definitions.definition: Made to be about the whole country instead of just a local area.
definitions.example: When a local school board election becomes about national issues like immigration, it's been nationalized.

definitions.definition: Super-sized group identities that combine many parts of a person's life—like where they live, who they marry, what they buy—into one big political label.
definitions.example: Being a Democrat or Republican now predicts your favorite news channel, your car brand, and even your pet preference.

definitions.definition: The process of people grouping into 'tribes' based on strong emotional loyalty, not just logical agreement.
definitions.example: Sports fans who hate the rival team even when they agree on other things.

definitions.definition: A moment when something changes direction or starts growing much faster.
definitions.example: The exact second a roller coaster stops climbing and starts dropping.

definitions.definition: Using computer programs to find patterns in large amounts of data.
definitions.example: A computer scanning millions of tweets to see which words are used most by each party.

definitions.definition: A specific point in time that marks an important change.
definitions.example: The date 'September 11, 2001' is a temporal marker for the start of the War on Terror.

definitions.definition: When two groups start using language in different ways, making it harder to understand each other.
definitions.example: Teenagers inventing slang that adults don't understand.

definitions.definition: Being loyal to your party mainly because you hate the other party, not because you love your own.
definitions.example: Voting for your team just to keep the other team out of power.

definitions.definition: Made stronger or more unified.
definitions.example: After the big win, the team's confidence consolidated into a winning streak.

definitions.definition: Able to grow from a small group to a large one without breaking.
definitions.example: A lemonade stand recipe that works for 10 cups and also for 10,000 cups is scalable.

definitions.definition: Getting members of a group to take action together based on their shared identity.
definitions.example: A church organizing a protest because members feel their values are threatened.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much knowing someone's opinion on one topic lets you predict their opinion on another topic.
definitions.example: If knowing someone is pro-choice lets you guess they are also pro-environment, that's high correlation.

definitions.definition: When members of different political parties vote similarly on laws.
definitions.example: A Democrat and a Republican both voting for the same education bill.

definitions.definition: A computer model that scores how liberal or conservative each member of Congress is based on their voting record.
definitions.example: A score of -1 means very liberal, +1 means very conservative, and 0 means moderate.

definitions.definition: Voting for candidates from different parties in the same election.
definitions.example: Voting for a Republican for president and a Democrat for senator.

definitions.definition: When people dislike members of the other political party as people, not just disagree with their ideas.
definitions.example: Not wanting your child to marry someone from the other party, even if you agree on policies.

definitions.definition: A survey tool where people rate how warm or cold they feel toward a group, from 0 (very cold) to 100 (very warm).
definitions.example: Rating your own party at 90 and the other party at 10 shows high affective polarization.

definitions.definition: Rules in physics that say the laws of nature stay the same even when you change certain things, like the way you measure energy.
definitions.example: Like how a game of chess is the same no matter what color the board is.

definitions.definition: The best scientific theory we have that explains all the known particles and forces in the universe (except gravity).
definitions.example: It's like the ultimate instruction manual for how the smallest building blocks of matter work.

definitions.definition: The underlying systems and arrangements that shape how things happen, not just the surface details.
definitions.example: The rules of a game (structural conditions) determine how players behave, not just their individual choices.

definitions.definition: When people's various identities (like religion, race, where they live) all line up with their political party.
definitions.example: A white evangelical Christian who lives in a rural area is very likely to be a Republican.

definitions.definition: Where a person puts themselves on a scale from very liberal to very conservative.
definitions.example: Saying 'I am a moderate' or 'I am very conservative' is ideological self-placement.

definitions.definition: Treating people unfairly because of their political party, similar to racial discrimination.
definitions.example: Not hiring someone because they are a Democrat or a Republican.

definitions.definition: Studies where scientists watch what people actually do, not just what they say.
definitions.example: Giving people money to share and seeing if they give more to their own party members.

definitions.definition: The strange fact that knowing someone's opinion on one issue lets you predict their opinion on all others, which shouldn't happen if people think independently.
definitions.example: If you know someone wants lower taxes, you can guess they also want stricter immigration laws, even though those are unrelated.

definitions.definition: A hidden factor that is not directly measured but explains why other things are connected.
definitions.example: Intelligence is a latent variable that explains why good grades in math and English often go together.

definitions.definition: When media chooses to show the most extreme members of the other party, making them seem scarier or weirder than they really are.
definitions.example: A news show always interviewing the angriest protester from the other side, not the calm ones.

definitions.definition: A set of persuasion techniques that target people's emotions and identities instead of their logic, named after Edward Bernays.
definitions.example: An ad that makes you feel patriotic instead of listing product features.

definitions.definition: Turned a concept into a specific, measurable action or process.
definitions.example: Turning 'customer satisfaction' into a survey with a 1-10 rating scale.

definitions.definition: When members of two different political parties work together to achieve something.
definitions.example: Democrats and Republicans writing a law together.

definitions.definition: A tax system where people who earn more money pay a higher percentage in taxes.
definitions.example: A person earning $1 million pays 37% tax, while someone earning $30,000 pays 12%.

definitions.definition: When people are pulled in different directions by conflicting loyalties or values.
definitions.example: A union member who supports the Democratic party but also wants lower taxes, which Republicans promise.

definitions.definition: Voting exactly the way your political party tells you to, without crossing over to the other side.
definitions.example: Every Republican voting 'no' and every Democrat voting 'yes' on a bill.

definitions.definition: A political strategy where a leader takes a position that is between the two parties' positions, to appeal to the middle.
definitions.example: A president supporting a smaller tax cut than Republicans want but a bigger one than Democrats want.

definitions.definition: The tendency for people to marry someone from the same political party.
definitions.example: A Democrat marrying another Democrat instead of a Republican.

definitions.definition: When people of the same type (like same party) live close together in certain areas.
definitions.example: Democrats clustering in cities and Republicans in rural areas.

definitions.definition: Topics that a person or group refuses to compromise on, no matter what.
definitions.example: For some, abortion rights are non-negotiable—they will never accept restrictions.

definitions.definition: A type of conservatism that supports using American military power to spread democracy around the world.
definitions.example: Supporting the Iraq War to remove Saddam Hussein and establish democracy.

definitions.definition: A rise to power, influence, or popularity.
definitions.example: The ascendancy of smartphones in the 2010s meant everyone had one.

definitions.definition: Stands for 'Republican In Name Only'—a insult used by some Republicans against others they think are not conservative enough.
definitions.example: Calling a Republican who supports some Democratic ideas a RINO.

definitions.definition: When someone runs against an existing officeholder from their own party in the primary election.
definitions.example: A conservative Republican running against a moderate Republican who is already in Congress.

definitions.definition: How far apart people feel from each other in terms of trust, understanding, and willingness to interact.
definitions.example: Feeling like you have nothing in common with someone from the other party is high social distance.

definitions.definition: A healthcare system where the government pays for all medical costs, like in Canada or the UK.
definitions.example: Medicare for All is a type of single-payer system.

definitions.definition: A phrase used to criticize a policy as going too far toward socialism, or government control of the economy.
definitions.example: Calling a new government healthcare program 'socialist overreach'.

definitions.definition: Permanent Normal Trade Relations—a status that gives a country normal trade benefits without yearly review.
definitions.example: Giving China PNTR meant American companies could trade with China without special restrictions.

definitions.definition: The process of a country joining the World Trade Organization, which sets global trade rules.
definitions.example: China's WTO accession in 2001 opened its markets to more foreign goods.

definitions.definition: A phrase meaning starting a small war to distract people from domestic problems.
definitions.example: Accusing a president of bombing another country just to change the news from a scandal at home.

definitions.definition: Official approval from Congress for the president to use military force.
definitions.example: Congress voting to authorize the president to go to war in Iraq.

definitions.definition: A measure of how two things change together, from -1 (opposite) to 0 (no relation) to 1 (perfect match).
definitions.example: Ice cream sales and temperature have a high positive correlation—when it's hot, both go up.

definitions.definition: A situation that cannot happen because it would break the rules of math.
definitions.example: Having a triangle with four sides is mathematically impossible.

definitions.definition: The authority of the president or governor to act without Congress's approval.
definitions.example: A president using an executive order to change immigration policy.

definitions.definition: A tactic in the Senate where a senator talks for a long time to delay or block a vote on a bill.
definitions.example: A senator reading a phone book for hours to stop a law from passing.

definitions.definition: A Senate rule change that allows a simple majority (51 votes) to end a filibuster, instead of the usual 60.
definitions.example: Using the nuclear option to confirm a Supreme Court justice with only 51 votes.

definitions.definition: The large group of people (about 67% of Americans) who are tired of political fighting and want compromise.
definitions.example: People who don't post about politics online but wish both sides would just get along.

definitions.definition: Focused on practical results rather than strict principles or ideology.
definitions.example: A pragmatic person would support a policy that works, even if it's not perfect according to their beliefs.

definitions.definition: The idea that the rules and processes used to make decisions should be fair and consistent.
definitions.example: Everyone getting the same chance to speak in a meeting is procedural fairness.

definitions.definition: The idea that resources and benefits in society should be shared fairly among all people.
definitions.example: Making sure rich and poor neighborhoods both get good schools is distributive justice.

definitions.definition: Freedom from interference by others, especially the government.
definitions.example: The freedom to say what you want without being arrested.

definitions.definition: Freedom to achieve your potential, which may require help from society or government.
definitions.example: The freedom to go to college, which requires affordable tuition and schools.

definitions.definition: A research method where you systematically count and categorize the content of media, like news shows or tweets.
definitions.example: Counting how many times each party is mentioned on Fox News vs. MSNBC.

definitions.definition: A pattern where the more you are exposed to something, the stronger the effect.
definitions.example: The more hours you watch partisan news, the more you dislike the other party.

definitions.definition: When a computer program (like on YouTube or Facebook) chooses what content to show you based on your past behavior.
definitions.example: After you watch one political video, the algorithm shows you more similar ones.

definitions.definition: Designing content to make people as angry or upset as possible, because that gets more clicks and shares.
definitions.example: A headline that says 'You won't believe what they did now!' to make you furious.

definitions.definition: A set of ideas from Sigmund Freud about how hidden desires and childhood experiences shape our behavior.
definitions.example: The idea that you buy a certain car because it makes you feel powerful, not because you need it.
